------------------------------------------
Hindu India when attacked by the barbarous aliens, met in its own characteristic way, the challenges against its cherished values of life, which it considered as eternal. This was done mainly by the galaxy of great saints from all parts of India and from the innumerable cults, groups and sects.
In this, the part played by the saints of Maharashtra was considerable.
Janārdana Svāmin was one such great saint.
Born in Cālīsgāv, a small village, in A.

, Janārdana was given a good एदुचतिओन् not only in the scriptures and secular sciences but also in the use of weapons, horse-riding and statecraft.
He was married to two girls at an early age. After his parents died, he took over the responsibilities of the family spending much of his time in worldly pursuits. However one strange spiritual experience in a temple where he had a vision of दत्तात्रेय, changed the course of his life completely. He received special instructions from a sage, नरसिṁह सरस्वती, in sādhanā (spiritual practice) under a sacred tree. He spent quite a few days there practising austerities and meditation.
A Muslim Navāb was the ruler of that area during those days. He recognised Janārdana’s great qualities and appointed him as the commander of the fort. Janārdana, by his efficient administration brought peace and prosperity to the people under his care.
He generally lived in धारेश्वर in Devagiri and used to hold his court there.
His biographers state that he would often visit a cave on the nearby hill and have the darśan (‘seeing’) of his chosen deity दत्तात्रेय. He had many disciples including the local Muslims and the Arabs.
Thursday was the day he had set apart for meditation and worship and hence was not available for any work. Noticing this, the Muslim Navāb had declared Thursday as the weekly holiday for all governmental work.
Another great saint of Maharashtra, Eknāth, was his chief disciple. It was at his command that Eknāth composed the Bhāgavata in Marāṭhī poetry.
Janārdana Svāmin had many psychic powers which he judiciously used when necessary, to help others.
He has composed quite a few अभङ्गस् (devotional songs) which are sung even today.
He passed away in A.

Janasthāna
------------------------------------------
One of the places connected with Śrī राम as mentioned in the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, जनस्थान was a part of the दण्डकारण्य forest. Śrī राम, सीता and लक्ष्मण lived here for quite a long time. Disfigurement of the ogress शूर्पणखा, decimation of Khara, Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras as also their army of 14,000 demons by Śrī राम, allurement of सीता by Mārīca in the guise of a golden deer, abduction of सीता by रावण are some of the important incidents of the story that took place here.
See also DAṆḌAKĀRAṆYA.

janana
(‘birth’)
------------------------------------------
This body, of which every living being is fond of, is subject to ṣaḍvikāras or six kinds of changes. जनन or birth is the first.
The word is also used for the extri-cation of the letters of a मन्त्र through the मातृकायन्त्र. See MANTRASAṀSKĀRA and MĀTṚKĀYANTRA for details.

Janmāṣṭamī
(‘the eighth day [on which] the birth [of Śrī कृष्ण occurred]’)
------------------------------------------
Janmāṣṭamī or Śrī कृष्ण-janmāṣtamī is perhaps the most popular and the most widely celebrated festival all over India as also among the Hindus living abroad. The very fact that the word ‘Janmāṣṭamī’ which has no reference to कृष्ण at all, means the birthday of Śrī कृष्ण, is a proof of this.
Śrī कृष्ण, like Śrī राम, इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु, has been commanding the love and affection, reverence and devotion, of millions of Hindus for millennia.
The problem of the historicity of कृष्ण, discussed by erudite scholars over the centuries, is not at all relevant to our study and exposition of the कृष्ण festival here. If a ‘person’ or a ‘personality’ has succeeded in capturing the psyche and ethos of an entire nation for numberless years, he is certainly the maker and shaper of history and not just a poor historical entity!
The birthday of Śrī कृष्ण, though mentioned as Śrāvaṇa Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī (associated with the रोहिणी नक्षत्र, the 4th asterism, comprising five स्तर्स्) is sometimes assigned to the month Bhādrapada or even to other months and dates, which may be assumed to refer to some older traditions. The date given here (eighth day in the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, usually in August/September) is now the universally accepted one.
If the aṣṭamī tithi and the रोहिणी नक्षत्र occur on the same day, it is doubly sacred and the vrata is observed on the same day. Otherwise, it is to be observed on the aṣṭamī day only. If both are spread over two days, the latter day is chosen for the observance.
Since कृष्ण was born at midnight, the observance of the vrata commences at midnight. ड़स्तिन्ग्, keeping vigil the whole night, worship of Lord कृष्ण, repeating or listening to the recitations from the Bhāgavata or hymns of praise on कृष्ण’s story and exploits, and, pāraṇā (ceremonial breaking of the fast)—these are the main items in the जन्माष्टमी vrata. The सङ्कल्प मन्त्र may mention the reward one wants (if the vrata is observed as kāmya or with desire) or it can be done for self-purification.
Some works giving more detailed instructions about the vrata advise the performer to devise a temporary sūtikāgṛha or delivery room! This caters to the popular sentiments even as the creche in Christianity does. The पूजा includes the performance of certain sacraments to be done at the birth of a child like the जातकर्म, and नामकरण or the naming ceremony.
Generally, the रोहिणी नक्षत्र falls on the next day which is observed as Jayantī or Śrī कृष्ण Jayantī. It may be observed either as a vrata or as an उत्सव, a festival, the latter being the rule.
Coming to the social aspects of the celebrations: In some parts of the country like Maharashtra, boys and common folk hang up pots full of curds and buttermilk, play underneath them, and get drenched by the curds and buttermilk running out of the holes made by the boys, in typical कृष्ण fashion! In some of the South Indian homes, some of the eatables prepared for the occasion, are hung on a frame at the top of the मण्डप (temporary shrine structure) and distributed among the devotees, especially the children, after the festivities.
The celebrations are held on a grand scale in all the कृष्ण temples, especially the ones in वृन्दाबन्, मथुरा (in Uttar Pradesh) and द्वारका (in Gujarat). Processions with कृष्ण images in cradles are a common sight.

Janaka
------------------------------------------
The king Nimi, the son of इक्ष्वाकु and grandson of वैवस्वत मनु, gave up his body due to the curse of the sage वसिष्ठ. Since there was chaos in the kingdom, people churned the body of Nimi and out came a person who was named ‘Videha,’ ‘Mithi’ and ‘Janaka’. He was crowned as the new king. Hereafter, all persons born in his lineage came to be known as Vaideha or Maithila or जनक.
The original name of the जनक of the Rāmāyaṇa was Sīradhvaja. When he was tilling his land as a part of the ceremony connected with the पुत्रकामेष्टि sacrifice he got a female baby inside a golden box. He named her ‘Sītā.’ His own daughter (born later) was Ūrmiḷā. His wife was Sumedhā.
When he arranged the स्वयṁवर (marriage by choice by the bride) of his daughter सीता, he had stipulated that whoever strung the Śivadhanus (the bow of शिव which was in his possession) would win her as his wife. Śrī राम did it and married सीता.
Janaka’s name appears in the Mahābhārata several times. His sage talks with पञ्चशिख (about spiritual wisdom), Sumedhā (on the need to follow the duties of a क्षत्त्रिय even after attaining ज्ञान or knowledge), Aśma (on धर्म in general) and कहोल have been given prominence in that epic.
His equanimity due to the attainment of spiritual wisdom has been described in the incident where he received the news of his capital मिथिला being reduced to ashes due to a great fire.
His conversation with the sage पराशर has now become well-known as the Parāśaragītā (Śāntiparva 290-298).
He stressed the importance of giving up āśā (desire) and mamatā (attachment) for attaining true happiness.
According to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4th Chapter) he received spiritual wisdom from the great sage याज्ञवल्क्य.
See also RĀMĀYAṆA.

janapada
(‘people’)
------------------------------------------
In the works on political science, every rājya or State is said to have seven aṅgas or constituents. जनपद (also called Rāṣṭra) is the third.
Janapada in effect means the people of the State.
Since the kingdom, the entire govern-mental system, is meant for the welfare of the people, they must be kept happy and contented. For this they need security and all opportunities for development. The primary means of achieving this is by giving them ड़ोओद्, clothing, shelter, health-care, एदुचतिओन् and avenues for employment. Hence, the king and his government must support and encourage all organizations of public service such as trade guilds, labour unions, educational institutions and self-government agencies like the pañcāyats. As far as possible, all welfare activities must be undertaken through them or with their co-operation.

Janaloka
------------------------------------------
Hindu mythological works describe fourteen worlds—six above this earth and seven below—as comprising this universe. Out of the worlds above the earth जनलोक is the fifth. Four types of divine beings live here. They have controlled and conquered the five elements (pañcamahā-bhūtas) and all the sense-organs. Their duration of life is two thousand kalpas (one कल्प = 3.32 billion human years).
According to one account it is millions of leagues away from the pole-star.

Janamejaya
(‘one who frightens his enemies even from his birth’)
------------------------------------------
Janamejaya was the first son of the king परीक्षित्, and the great grandson of अर्जुन, the famous Pāṇḍava hero. He took over as the king after परीक्षित् died of snake-bite. (See PARĪKṢIT for details.)
Vapuṣṭamā, the daughter of Suvarman (king of काशी), was his queen from whom he had two sons—Śatānīka and Śaṅkukarṇa.
After hearing the entire महाभारत story from the sage वैशम्पायन and having come to know of his ड़थेर्’s death by तक्षक’s bite (See TAKṢAKA.) he started the Sarpayāga—asacrifice to exterminate the entire race of serpents.
The sages Caṇḍabhārgava, Piṅgala, जैमिनि and Aṅgirasa were the four principal priests who assisted him in this sacrifice.
As the sacrifice progressed, serpents in their thousands started falling into the fire and were getting destroyed.
During the final stages, when तक्षक was being forced towards the sacrificial fire, the young sage आस्तिक arrived on the scene and successfully stopped the massacre of the reptiles by convincing the king जनमेजय through his sweet speech and powerful लोगिच्. The king immediately stopped the holocaust.
Four more kings during the different periods of ancient Hindu history were also known by this name.
See also ĀSTIKA.

Jānaśruti
------------------------------------------
Jānaśruti was a king. He was the son of Janaśruta and the grandson of पुत्र. Hence he was known as Pautrāyaṇa also.
This जानश्रुति Pautrāyaṇa was well-known for his generosity, especially for giving ड़ोओद् to the needy, through the numerous free kitchens all over his country.
One night, when he was resting on the terrace of his palace, he heard the conversation between two swans which were flying over his head. While one swan warned the other not to cross the brilliant light above जानश्रुति’s head lest it be harmed, the latter spoke derisively of him, comparing him to the sage रैक्व who was far superior to him.
Jānaśruti who was upset by this conversation between the birds, sent his men in the morning to search for रैक्व. They finally found him sitting under a cart and scratching his skin affected by scabies.
When the king approached रैक्व for spiritual wisdom, the sage taught him what is known as Saṁvargavidyā.
